items.primary_i_can: I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.
items.evidence_job: Navigate a connected vector stimulus by reading arrow direction/relative length, identifying needed quantities, and planning how the resultant connects to motion change.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.3: force vectors, same/opposite-direction combination, resultant from scaled arrows; Physics Framework: representations carry evidence.
items.student_text:
Two students pull a low-friction sled. The force arrows are drawn to the same scale:

6 N ←──── [sled] ──────────→ 14 N

(a) Which force is larger, and what feature of the diagram shows that?
(b) Find the resultant force, including direction.
(c) A classmate says the two forces cancel because they point in opposite directions. Evaluate that claim.
(d) Without calculating acceleration, predict the direction in which the sled’s velocity will begin to change and explain which earlier result your prediction uses.
items.student_html:
Two students pull a low-friction sled. The force arrows are drawn to the same scale:

6 N ←──── [sled] ──────────→ 14 N

(a) Which force is larger, and what feature of the diagram shows that?
(b) Find the resultant force, including direction.
(c) A classmate says the two forces cancel because they point in opposite directions. Evaluate that claim.
(d) Without calculating acceleration, predict the direction in which the sled’s velocity will begin to change and explain which earlier result your prediction uses.
items.answer: (a) The 14 N rightward force is larger; its arrow is longer. (b) 8 N right. (c) Incorrect; opposite directions cancel only equal amounts, leaving 8 N right. (d) The velocity changes toward the right; this conclusion depends on the rightward resultant from part (b).
items.solution_text: Because vector direction matters, subtract the opposite force magnitudes: 14 N − 6 N = 8 N to the right. The nonzero resultant points right, so the motion changes in that direction.
items.solution_html: Because vector direction matters, subtract the opposite force magnitudes: 14 N − 6 N = 8 N to the right. The nonzero resultant points right, so the motion changes in that direction.

items.primary_i_can: I can explain why force is a vector quantity.
items.evidence_job: Use arrow direction and length as meaningful vector features and critique a representation that treats a force arrow as a scalar label.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.3: force vectors, same/opposite-direction combination, resultant from scaled arrows; Physics Framework: representations carry evidence.
items.student_text: Two diagrams both label a force ‘8 N.’ Diagram A shows a long arrow right; Diagram B shows a short arrow left. A student says they represent the same vector because both say 8 N. What is wrong with the representation/reasoning?
items.student_html: Two diagrams both label a force ‘8 N.’ Diagram A shows a long arrow right; Diagram B shows a short arrow left. A student says they represent the same vector because both say 8 N. What is wrong with the representation/reasoning?
items.answer: A force vector requires both magnitude and direction, and a scaled arrow should use length consistently; opposite directions are different vectors and inconsistent lengths cannot both represent the same 8 N on one scale.
items.solution_text: Force is a vector. Arrow direction carries direction information and arrow length carries relative magnitude when the diagram is scaled.
items.solution_html: Force is a vector. Arrow direction carries direction information and arrow length carries relative magnitude when the diagram is scaled.

items.student_text: A student draws a 5 N eastward force and a 5 N westward force using arrows that both point east. Critique the drawing.
items.student_html: A student draws a 5 N eastward force and a 5 N westward force using arrows that both point east. Critique the drawing.
items.answer: One arrow must point west; equal magnitudes do not erase the direction requirement.
items.solution_text: The magnitude 5 N is only part of the vector. The arrows must point in the actual force directions.
items.solution_html: The magnitude 5 N is only part of the vector. The arrows must point in the actual force directions.

items.primary_i_can: I can combine forces acting in the same direction or opposite directions.
items.evidence_job: Combine same/opposite-direction forces from a physical situation and interpret the sign/direction of the net force.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.3: force vectors, same/opposite-direction combination, resultant from scaled arrows; Physics Framework: representations carry evidence.
items.student_text: Two students push a crate to the right with 18 N and 27 N while friction pushes 15 N left. Use F_net = sum of rightward forces − sum of leftward forces to find the net force and direction.
items.student_html: Two students push a crate to the right with 18 N and 27 N while friction pushes 15 N left. Use F_net = sum of rightward forces − sum of leftward forces to find the net force and direction.
items.solution_text: F_net = (18 + 27) − 15 = 30 N. The positive/rightward side is larger, so the net force is 30 N right.
items.solution_html: F_net = (18 + 27) − 15 = 30 N. The positive/rightward side is larger, so the net force is 30 N right.

items.student_text: A sled is pulled 42 N left while another person pulls 17 N right. Find the net force and direction.
items.student_html: A sled is pulled 42 N left while another person pulls 17 N right. Find the net force and direction.
items.solution_text: Opposite forces subtract. 42 − 17 = 25 N, toward the larger leftward force.
items.solution_html: Opposite forces subtract. 42 − 17 = 25 N, toward the larger leftward force.

items.primary_i_can: I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.
items.evidence_job: Read force magnitudes/directions from an actual vector diagram and determine the resultant while preserving direction meaning.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.3: force vectors, same/opposite-direction combination, resultant from scaled arrows; Physics Framework: representations carry evidence.
items.student_text: Scaled vector diagram: 4 N ← [cart] ─────────→ 11 N. Read the diagram and determine the resultant force, including direction.
items.student_html: Scaled vector diagram: 4 N ← [cart] ─────────→ 11 N. Read the diagram and determine the resultant force, including direction.
items.solution_text: The arrows are opposite, so subtract their magnitudes: 11 − 4 = 7 N. The longer/larger arrow points right.
items.solution_html: The arrows are opposite, so subtract their magnitudes: 11 − 4 = 7 N. The longer/larger arrow points right.

items.student_html: Scaled vector diagram: 13 N ←──────── [sled] ───→ 5 N. Determine the resultant force and direction.
items.solution_text: 13 − 5 = 8 N, in the direction of the larger leftward vector.

items.student_text: A tug-of-war team pulls 70 N right. What leftward force is needed for the resultant to be 15 N right? Use F_net = F_right − F_left.
items.student_html: A tug-of-war team pulls 70 N right. What leftward force is needed for the resultant to be 15 N right? Use F_net = F_right − F_left.

items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.3: force vectors, same/opposite-direction combination, resultant from scaled arrows; Physics Framework: representations carry evidence.
items.student_text: A cart is pushed 48 N left. What rightward force would make the net force 12 N left?
items.student_html: A cart is pushed 48 N left. What rightward force would make the net force 12 N left?
items.solution_text: For 12 N left, the leftward side must exceed the rightward side by 12 N: 48 − F_right = 12, so F_right = 36 N.
items.solution_html: For 12 N left, the leftward side must exceed the rightward side by 12 N: 48 − F_right = 12, so F_right = 36 N.
